newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark flat, dlr/yen lower after US May durables.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark flat, dlr/yen lower after US May durables.

text.p: The dollar was virtually unchanged versus the mark and sharply lower versus the yen following an unexpected 0.6-percent drop in May U.S. durable goods orders that confirmed market sentiment U.S. interest rates will remain steady in July, traders said.
"Initially, the durables goods report should pressure the dollar," a trader at a French bank in New York said.
"Dollar/yen should resume its slide and may retest the overnight low at 113.20/30. Dollar/mark should remain in a narrow range, between 1.7150/80 on the downside and 1.7270 on the upside."
At 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 1.7231/36 mark versus 1.7240/50 at the close on Tuesday, and at 113.62/72 yen versus 114.90/95.
The dollar had fallen sharply overnight on Japan's stronger-than-expected tankan report that a number of analysts said was pointing to higher interest rates in Japan.
"A lot, for the dollar, will depend on what bonds and the Dow (Jones industrial average) do today," the trader added.
Despite the surprisingly weak durables goods report, the 30-year Treasury bond was down 10/32 at 98.26, yielding 6.72 percent.

Treasury dealers said the credit market has long priced in the absence of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on July 1-2 and that the durables goods did not bring any new information on that front.
Treasuries were further pressured by the Treasury auction of five-year notes later today.
U.S. stocks were also expected to open somewhat lower after posting strong gains on Tuesday.
"With prospects of a rate hike in Japan, the interest rate differential is less supportive for dollar/yen, already weakened by Japan's large trade surplus," the trader said.
"Dollar/mark is fairly well contained," said Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal.

"On dollar/yen, there seems to be a lot of interest in the options market for yen calls. For that reason, I don't think the downside for dollar/yen is very well supported," Benfer further said. "Maybe, the dollar should go another yen lower before finding real support."

The yen, lifted overnight by news of improving business conditions in Japan, got an added boost this morning from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto who said "the yen has no wish to be relegated to a local currency."
Hashimoto was speaking in The Hague where he is attending a European Union (EU)-Japan summit focusing on trade.

Hashimoto roiled U.S. financial markets on Monday with remarks made in New York about the need for U.S.-Japan foreign exchange cooperation and references to Japan's temptation to sell U.S. Treasuries to deal with foreign exchange volatility.
Traders said the yen, which also scored good gains versus the mark, is likely to lead the market action today.
Mark/yen retreated overnight and is expected to test intermediate support at 65.80 during the New York session, which should help dollar/mark but pressure dollar/yen.
Traders cited another reason for a relatively positive dollar/mark near-term outlook -- prospects of a rate cut in Italy that lifted the Italian debt and pushed the lira higher versus the mark.
Also in morning trading, the dollar was quoted at 1.4380/90 Swiss francs, unchanged from the close on Tuesday, and at Canadian $1.3950/55 versus C$1.3905/10.
Sterling was quoted at $1.6648/53 versus $1.6690/00. The Australian dollar traded at $0.7511/16 versus $0.7505/10.
((-- Isabelle Clary, 212-859-1666))
